title: Fennel and the Fierce Gale
markdown:
Fennel kept his burrow in the thyme that clung to the Elder Cliffs. The rooms were low and dry. The walls smelled of leaf and salt. Most evenings Ivo the sheepdog stretched across the threshold like a living door, and Fennel counted that weight as the safest thing he knew.

The sea below was a neighbour he preferred not to meet. From the entrance the drop ran straight into white water. Fennel could tidy a store of seeds, mend a grass mat, and still keep his eyes on the inner dark of the burrow. Heights made his paws sweat. He had never pretended otherwise.

On the third evening of a rising wind, the Whispering Gale came in from the west. It did not arrive as weather. It arrived as a hand that tested the stone. Thyme tore from the lip of the path. The first roar found the burrow mouth and turned Fennel’s small rooms into a drum.

Ivo lifted his head. Old Man Thistlewick, the cliff badger, had warned them for years: when the Gale chose a night, only one shelter held. It lay below the lookout hut, carved by older paws than theirs. The map that named the turn sat in that hut, on the sharpest edge of the cliff.

Fennel’s home would not last the full storm. He knew that as clearly as he knew the drop. He also knew the hut stood where the path thinned to a ribbon of wet rock.

They left because staying would finish the burrow before midnight.

The path took them at once. Wind shoved their shoulders toward the sea. Spray climbed the cliff and salted Fennel’s whiskers. The lookout hut stood ahead, a gaunt box against a sky the colour of a bruise. Each step asked Fennel to look down. He would not. He watched Ivo’s paws instead, the dark pads finding holds that did not crumble.

Halfway along, scree slid under his heel. For one long breath the world tilted. The chasm opened in his mind like a mouth. He stopped. The burrow, ruined or not, still felt kinder than this. Ivo waited without a sound. Fennel set his feet again and went on, not because the fear had left, but because the wind had begun to peel the turf from the path behind them.

The hut’s door hung on one hinge. Inside, the gale spoke through broken panes and lifted dust in pale sheets. A rickety table had already walked itself toward the far wall. Fennel’s eyes jumped from beam to beam. He needed the map. He also needed the floor to stay still.

It did not. The hut leaned. Through a missing plank he saw mist turning in the drop, and the old dizziness took him by the throat. He froze with his paws spread on the boards. Cold sweat stood in his fur.

Ivo sat against his flank. The dog’s warmth was ordinary and stubborn. Amber eyes held Fennel’s until the room narrowed back to wood and dust. Together they looked again. Under a splintered beam, yellowed and rolled, the map waited as if it had been listening.

Fennel lunged and caught it. The parchment crackled in his grip. For a moment he thought the night had given them what they asked.

Then a wall of the hut peeled outward. The Gale stood in the gap, huge and close. Fennel unrolled the map with shaking paws. The mark he wanted was not a cave beside the path. It was a steep descent down the cliff face, into the very weather they had run from.

That was the cost of the finding. He pictured himself on the rock, wind taking his ears, the sea waiting with a patience he could not match. His legs went thin. The hut’s wet wood pressed his fur. Salt and damp earth filled his nose until he could taste them.

He thought of the burrow tearing from the cliff. He thought of Ivo still beside him, not pushing, only remaining.

“Ivo,” Fennel said, and the wind stole half the word. “We must.”

They left through the ruined doorway.

The descent was a conversation with stone. Fennel learned the grain of each hold by touch. He did not look at the water. He looked at Ivo’s shoulders, at the next crack, at the map’s damp edge between his teeth when he needed both paws. Fear travelled with him like a second heartbeat. It did not choose the next step. He did.

Sea-grass hung in a curtain over a narrow mouth in the cliff. They pushed through it and fell onto a floor that was dry and strangely warm. Above them the Whispering Gale broke in full. The roar filled the world. Inside the shelter it became a distant thunder, as if the storm had been asked to wait in another room.

Fennel curled against Ivo’s side. The map lay between them, its ink blurred by spray. Outside, a gust rattled the sea-grass with the same voice the cliff-face had used. The old prickle rose in him. He set his paws on the cool earth and breathed until the prickle passed.

He was still a bunny who disliked the drop. He was also the bunny who had walked it, and who would sleep now with the storm held at the door.
characters: Fennel (a cliff-path bunny), Ivo (a loyal sheepdog)
